claim: There was a significant reduction in hippocampal volume bilaterally during the acute stage measured by T2-weighted scans.
source: There was a significant reduction in hippocampal volume bilaterally during the acute stage measured by T2-weighted scans (Figure 1A), histologically (Figure 1B) and deformation-based morphometry of T1-weighted structural MRI scans (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by T2-weighted scan data shown in Figure 1A and referenced in the text.

claim: There was a significant reduction in hippocampal volume bilaterally during the acute stage measured histologically.
source: There was a significant reduction in hippocampal volume bilaterally during the acute stage measured by T2-weighted scans (Figure 1A), histologically (Figure 1B) and deformation-based morphometry of T1-weighted structural MRI scans (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1B and referenced in the text.

claim: There was a significant reduction in hippocampal volume bilaterally during the acute stage measured by deformation-based morphometry of T1-weighted structural MRI scans.
source: There was a significant reduction in hippocampal volume bilaterally during the acute stage measured by T2-weighted scans (Figure 1A), histologically (Figure 1B) and deformation-based morphometry of T1-weighted structural MRI scans (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by deformation-based morphometry data shown in Figures 1C-D and referenced in the text.

claim: All three analysis methods gave consistent results for hippocampal volume reduction.
source: All three analysis methods gave consistent results.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of results from T2-weighted scans, histology, and deformation-based morphometry.

claim: Lesions were mostly bilateral and extensive.
source: Lesions were mostly bilateral and extensive, although there was some apparent sparing of the right hippocampus posteriorly across the five monkeys (Figure 1; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: There was some apparent sparing of the right hippocampus posteriorly across the five monkeys.
source: Lesions were mostly bilateral and extensive, although there was some apparent sparing of the right hippocampus posteriorly across the five monkeys (Figure 1; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: The apparent sparing of the posterior part of the hippocampus is likely an under-estimation of the amount of damage due to partial volume effects.
source: However, this is likely an under-estimation of the amount of damage in the posterior part of the hippocampus, which is narrower and therefore more susceptible to partial volume effects with neighbouring tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about technical limitations of imaging narrow structures.

claim: Across all pairwise connections between brain regions, there was an overall increase in the functional connectivity strength over the acute stage.
source: Across all pairwise connections between brain regions, there was an overall increase in the functional connectivity strength over the acute stage (t6318 = 9.37, p = 1×10−22), and a decrease over the chronic stage (t6318 = −16.85, p = 2×10−62).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with t-test results showing p = 1×10−22.

claim: Across all pairwise connections between brain regions, there was a decrease in functional connectivity strength over the chronic stage.
source: Across all pairwise connections between brain regions, there was an overall increase in the functional connectivity strength over the acute stage (t6318 = 9.37, p = 1×10−22), and a decrease over the chronic stage (t6318 = −16.85, p = 2×10−62).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with t-test results showing p = 2×10−62.

claim: The hippocampus is a key part of the episodic memory circuit.
source: The hippocampus is a key part of the episodic memory circuit, but the impact of lesions restricted to the hippocampus itself is not always large (Malkova and Mishkin, 2003; Zola-Morgan and Squire, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The impact of lesions restricted to the hippocampus itself is not always large.
source: The hippocampus is a key part of the episodic memory circuit, but the impact of lesions restricted to the hippocampus itself is not always large (Malkova and Mishkin, 2003; Zola-Morgan and Squire, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Malkova and Mishkin (2003) and Zola-Morgan and Squire (1986).

claim: The episodic memory circuit is widespread in nature.
source: Because of the widespread nature of the episodic memory circuit (Aggleton and Brown, 1999), we hypothesized that this may be due to functional plasticity in the form of intact brain regions compensating for the damaged area (a process we previously showed to be critically dependent on cholinergic inputs to inferior temporal cortex following hippocampal disconnection (Browning et al., 2010; Croxson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aggleton and Brown (1999).

claim: Functional plasticity in the form of intact brain regions compensating for damaged areas is critically dependent on cholinergic inputs to inferior temporal cortex following hippocampal disconnection.
source: Because of the widespread nature of the episodic memory circuit (Aggleton and Brown, 1999), we hypothesized that this may be due to functional plasticity in the form of intact brain regions compensating for the damaged area (a process we previously showed to be critically dependent on cholinergic inputs to inferior temporal cortex following hippocampal disconnection (Browning et al., 2010; Croxson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Browning et al., 2010; Croxson et al., 2012).

claim: Hubness and pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity significantly predicted the cortex-wide pattern of acute changes in network participation coefficient.
source: The model significantly predicted the cortex-wide pattern of acute changes in network participation coefficient, explaining over half of the variance (F2,75 = 42.24, p = 5×10−13, r2 = 0.53, Figure 3B). Hubness (t73 = −5.70, p = 2×10−7), and pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity (t73 = −5.25, p = 1×10−6) were significantly associated with a drop in network participation coefficient over the acute stage (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing F2,75 = 42.24, p = 5×10−13, r2 = 0.53, with individual predictors showing significant t-statistics.

claim: The model explained over half of the variance in acute changes in network participation coefficient.
source: The model significantly predicted the cortex-wide pattern of acute changes in network participation coefficient, explaining over half of the variance (F2,75 = 42.24, p = 5×10−13, r2 = 0.53, Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the reported r2 = 0.53.

claim: Hubness was significantly associated with a drop in network participation coefficient over the acute stage.
source: Hubness (t73 = −5.70, p = 2×10−7), and pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity (t73 = −5.25, p = 1×10−6) were significantly associated with a drop in network participation coefficient over the acute stage (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = −5.70, p = 2×10−7.

claim: Pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity was significantly associated with a drop in network participation coefficient over the acute stage.
source: Hubness (t73 = −5.70, p = 2×10−7), and pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity (t73 = −5.25, p = 1×10−6) were significantly associated with a drop in network participation coefficient over the acute stage (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = −5.25, p = 1×10−6.

claim: Neuron density was not a significant predictor of acute changes in network participation coefficient.
source: Neither neuron density (t73 = −1.04, p = 0.29) nor non-neuronal cell density showed a significant association (t73 = −0.55, p = 0.59).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = −1.04, p = 0.29.

claim: Non-neuronal cell density was not a significant predictor of acute changes in network participation coefficient.
source: Neither neuron density (t73 = −1.04, p = 0.29) nor non-neuronal cell density showed a significant association (t73 = −0.55, p = 0.59).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = −0.55, p = 0.59.

claim: Non-neuronal cell density was significantly associated with a rise in network participation coefficient over the chronic stage.
source: The model significantly predicted the cortex-wide pattern of chronic stage changes in network participation coefficient (F2,75 = 24.3, p = 7×10−9, r2 = 0.39, Figure 3E). Non-neuronal cell density was significantly associated with a rise in network participation coefficient over the chronic stage (t73 = 4.70, p = 1×10−5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = 4.70, p = 1×10−5.

claim: Hubness was significantly associated with a drop in network participation coefficient during the chronic stage.
source: As in the acute phase, hubness was significantly associated with a drop in network participation coefficient during the chronic stage (t73 = −4.93, p – 4 × 10−6) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = −4.93, p = 4 × 10−6.

claim: Neuron density was not a significant predictor of chronic changes in network participation coefficient.
source: Neither neuron density (t73 = 1.57, p = 0.12) nor hippocampal functional connectivity (t73 = 1.24, p = 0.22) were significant predictors of chronic stage network participation changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = 1.57, p = 0.12.

claim: Hippocampal functional connectivity was not a significant predictor of chronic changes in network participation coefficient.
source: Neither neuron density (t73 = 1.57, p = 0.12) nor hippocampal functional connectivity (t73 = 1.24, p = 0.22) were significant predictors of chronic stage network participation changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = 1.24, p = 0.22.

claim: Hubness significantly predicted the cortex-wide pattern of acute stage changes in within-module functional connectivity.
source: A model with hubness as the lone predictor (identified with stepwise regression) significantly predicted the cortex-wide pattern of acute stage changes in within-module functional connectivity (Figure 4B; Figure 4C, F1,76 = 10.25, p = 0.002, r2 = 0.12, hubness t73 = −3.20, p = 0.002, neuron density t73 = −1.39, p = 0.168, non-neuronal cell density t73 = −0.92, p = 0.359, pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity t73 = −0.28, p = 0.782).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing F1,76 = 10.25, p = 0.002, r2 = 0.12.

claim: Neuron density was a significant predictor of a drop in within-module functional connectivity during the chronic stage.
source: The stepwise regression model significantly predicted the cortex-wide pattern of chronic stage changes in within-module functional connectivity (F3,74 = 7.68, p = 0.0002, r2 = 0.24, Figure 4E). Neuron density (t73 = −2.54, p = 0.013) was a significant predictor of a drop in within-module functional connectivity during the chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = −2.54, p = 0.013.

claim: Pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity was associated with a chronic stage increase in within-module functional connectivity.
source: In contrast, pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity was associated with a chronic stage increase in within-module functional connectivity (t73 = 4.04, p = 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = 4.04, p = 0.0001.

claim: Non-neuronal cell density was not included in the final model for chronic changes in within-module functional connectivity.
source: Non-neuronal cell density was not included in the final model (t73 = −1.33, p = 0.19).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t73 = −1.33, p = 0.19.

claim: None of the four predictors significantly predicted acute stage changes in grey matter volume.
source: None of the four predictors significantly predicted acute stage changes in grey matter volume (neuron density: t73 = 1.10, p = 0.27, non-neuronal cell density: t73 = 0.40, p = 0.69, hubness: t73 = 1.27, p = 0.21, hippocampal functional connectivity: t73 = −0.11, p = 0.91) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing all p-values > 0.05.

claim: Pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity was the only significant predictor of chronic stage changes to grey matter volume.
source: The stepwise regression model for chronic stage changes to grey matter volume included only pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity in the final model (F1,76 = 16.39, r2 = 0.17, t73 = −4.05, p = 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing F1,76 = 16.39, r2 = 0.17, t73 = −4.05, p = 0.0001.

claim: During the acute stage, there were very limited volumetric decreases in the medial septum, amygdala and dorsal premotor cortex.
source: During the acute stage, there were very limited volumetric decreases in the medial septum, amygdala and dorsal premotor cortex. No increases survived thresholding (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by deformation-based morphometry analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No volumetric increases survived thresholding during the acute stage.
source: During the acute stage, there were very limited volumetric decreases in the medial septum, amygdala and dorsal premotor cortex. No increases survived thresholding (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by deformation-based morphometry analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At the chronic stage, volumetric decreases were observed in the medial septum.
source: At the chronic stage, we still saw decreases in the medial septum, but also a larger range of decreases.
evidence: The claim is supported by deformation-based morphometry analysis.

claim: At the chronic stage, volumetric decreases were observed in areas monosynaptically connected with the hippocampus including the medial orbitofrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex and posterior parahippocampal cortex.
source: Some of these were also in areas that are monosynaptically connected with the hippocampus: the medial orbitofrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex and posterior parahippocampal cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by deformation-based morphometry analysis and anatomical connectivity knowledge.

claim: At the chronic stage, there were volumetric decreases in the anterior prefrontal cortex (medial and lateral), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, dorsal striatum, visual cortex and superior temporal cortex.
source: There were also more extensive volumetric decreases, in the anterior prefrontal cortex (medial and lateral), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, dorsal striatum, visual cortex and superior temporal cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by deformation-based morphometry analysis.

claim: At the chronic stage, there were volumetric increases in the cerebellum, midbrain and premotor cortex.
source: There were also volumetric increases in the cerebellum, midbrain and premotor cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by deformation-based morphometry analysis.

claim: The chronic stage volumetric changes did not survive multiple comparisons correction.
source: These results did not survive multiple comparisons correction (possibly due to our small sample size), so these changes should be viewed with this caveat in mind.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated regarding the statistical significance of the results.

claim: Four modules were identified: orbitofrontal cortex/anterior temporal lobe, posterior temporal, parieto-occipital and dorsal frontal.
source: Four modules were identified, orbitofrontal cortex/anterior temporal lobe, posterior temporal, parieto-occipital and dorsal frontal.
evidence: The claim is based on module detection analysis using the Louvain algorithm.

claim: The parieto-occipital module is highly connected to the three other modules in the pre-lesion network.
source: The parieto-occipital module (orange) is highly connected to the three other modules.
evidence: The claim is based on force-directed graph representation of functional connectivity data.

claim: At 12 months post-lesion, the parieto-occipital module becomes dramatically dispersed.
source: At 12 months after the lesion however, this module (orange) becomes dramatically dispersed.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of within-module functional connectivity changes shown in force-directed graphs.

claim: During the acute stage, there is a significant difference between modules in within-module functional connectivity changes.
source: During the acute stage, (Figure 6C), there is not a large drop in within-module functional connectivity, although there is a significant difference between modules (F3,76=19.54, p = 4×10−9), with the parieto-occipital module dispersing somewhat, and the dorsal frontal and OFC/anterior temporal modules increasing their within-module functional connectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing F3,76=19.54, p = 4×10−9.

claim: During the chronic stage, there is a drop in within-module functional connectivity across all modules.
source: During the chronic stage (Figure 6D), there is a drop in within-module functional connectivity across all modules, with by far the greatest dispersion occurring in the parieto-occipital module (F3,76=41.86, p = 4×10−16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing F3,76=41.86, p = 4×10−16.

claim: The greatest dispersion during the chronic stage occurred in the parieto-occipital module.
source: During the chronic stage (Figure 6D), there is a drop in within-module functional connectivity across all modules, with by far the greatest dispersion occurring in the parieto-occipital module (F3,76=41.86, p = 4×10−16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and visual representation in Figure 6D.

claim: The dispersion of the parieto-occipital module led to a drop in connectivity between the modules.
source: The dispersion of the parieto-occipital module, which previously acted as a link between other modules, also led to a drop in connectivity between the modules, as seen by an increase in the modularity during the chronic stage (pre-lesion: 0.33, 3 months post-lesion: 0.34, 12 months post-lesion: 0.49; F2,297=60230, p~0).
evidence: The claim is supported by modularity measurements showing an increase from 0.33 pre-lesion to 0.49 at 12 months post-lesion.

claim: Modularity increased during the chronic stage from 0.34 at 3 months post-lesion to 0.49 at 12 months post-lesion.
source: The dispersion of the parieto-occipital module, which previously acted as a link between other modules, also led to a drop in connectivity between the modules, as seen by an increase in the modularity during the chronic stage (pre-lesion: 0.33, 3 months post-lesion: 0.34, 12 months post-lesion: 0.49; F2,297=60230, p~0).
evidence: The claim is supported by modularity measurements at different time points.

claim: There were always fewer modules at 12 months after the lesion compared to the pre-lesion scan, at all values of lambda tested.
source: There were always fewer modules at 12 months after the lesion compared to the pre-lesion scan, at all values of lambda tested (range 0.8–1.4).
evidence: The claim is based on module detection analysis across a range of resolution parameters.

claim: Neuron density was positively associated with hubness.
source: A model containing both neuron and non-neuronal cell density significantly predicted hubness (F2,75 = 6.18, r2 = 0.14, p = 0.003). Neuron density was positively associated with hubness (t = 3.49, p = 0.008), while non-neuronal cell density was negatively associated with hubness (t = −2.19, p = 0.032).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t = 3.49, p = 0.008.

claim: Non-neuronal cell density was negatively associated with hubness.
source: A model containing both neuron and non-neuronal cell density significantly predicted hubness (F2,75 = 6.18, r2 = 0.14, p = 0.003). Neuron density was positively associated with hubness (t = 3.49, p = 0.008), while non-neuronal cell density was negatively associated with hubness (t = −2.19, p = 0.032).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing t = −2.19, p = 0.032.

claim: Pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity was highly correlated with anatomical connectivity measures in the original CoCoMac Atlas.
source: Hippocampal functional connectivity measured in the current study was highly correlated with anatomical connectivity measures in both the original (r = 0.54, p = 2.2×10−7) and enhanced versions of the CoCoMac Atlas (r = 0.60, p = 3.6×10−9).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis showing r = 0.54, p = 2.2×10−7.

claim: Pre-lesion hippocampal functional connectivity was highly correlated with anatomical connectivity measures in the enhanced CoCoMac Atlas.
source: Hippocampal functional connectivity measured in the current study was highly correlated with anatomical connectivity measures in both the original (r = 0.54, p = 2.2×10−7) and enhanced versions of the CoCoMac Atlas (r = 0.60, p = 3.6×10−9).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis showing r = 0.60, p = 3.6×10−9.

claim: The strongest functional connectivity of the hippocampus was with medial and ventral temporal regions that are in close proximity to the hippocampus.
source: The strongest functional connectivity was with medial and ventral temporal regions that are in close proximity to the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of pre-lesion resting-state fMRI data.

claim: Dorsal frontal regions showed a slight negative correlation with the hippocampus.
source: In contrast, dorsal frontal regions showed a slight negative correlation with the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of pre-lesion resting-state fMRI data.

claim: Distant grey matter degeneration is a common anatomical consequence of a lesion.
source: Distant grey matter degeneration, and a loss of anatomical connectivity of grey matter areas not directly affected by the lesion are common anatomical consequences of a lesion (Catani and ffytche, 2005; Zaczek et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Catani and ffytche (2005) and Zaczek et al. (1980).

claim: A loss of anatomical connectivity of grey matter areas not directly affected by the lesion is a common anatomical consequence of a lesion.
source: Distant grey matter degeneration, and a loss of anatomical connectivity of grey matter areas not directly affected by the lesion are common anatomical consequences of a lesion (Catani and ffytche, 2005; Zaczek et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Catani and ffytche (2005) and Zaczek et al. (1980).

claim: The extent of functional disconnection of intact regions is associated with the degree of behavioral impairment following a lesion.
source: In addition, the extent of functional disconnection of intact regions is associated with the degree of behavioral impairment following a lesion (Corbetta et al., 2005; He et al., 2007) even if the areas remain structurally connected (van Meer et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corbetta et al. (2005) and He et al. (2007).

claim: Functional disconnection can occur even if areas remain structurally connected.
source: In addition, the extent of functional disconnection of intact regions is associated with the degree of behavioral impairment following a lesion (Corbetta et al., 2005; He et al., 2007) even if the areas remain structurally connected (van Meer et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to van Meer et al. (2010).

claim: Some brain areas adapt by altering their connectivity patterns and increasing their connections with other, often unaffected areas.
source: Conversely, some brain areas adapt by altering their connectivity patterns and increasing their connections with other, often unaffected areas (Yogarajah et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yogarajah et al. (2010).

claim: Currently, there is no quantitative way of predicting how unlesioned brain areas will adapt to injury elsewhere.
source: Currently, there is no quantitative way of predicting how unlesioned brain areas will adapt to injury elsewhere.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Much recovery occurs in the first few weeks following an injury.
source: Much recovery occurs in the first few weeks following an injury, but functional improvements may continue until much later (Berthier et al., 2011; Smania et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berthier et al. (2011) and Smania et al. (2010).

claim: Functional improvements may continue until much later than the first few weeks following an injury.
source: Much recovery occurs in the first few weeks following an injury, but functional improvements may continue until much later (Berthier et al., 2011; Smania et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berthier et al. (2011) and Smania et al. (2010).

claim: The microstructural consequences of brain injury can vary dramatically at different times following injury in rodents.
source: Studies in rodents have shown that the microstructural consequences of brain injury can vary dramatically at different times following injury, which could have serious implications for potential treatment strategies (Hoskison et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoskison et al. (2009).

claim: Small animal models of brain injury are not optimal for investigating chronic plastic changes due to the short lifespan of rodents.
source: However, small animal models of brain injury are not optimal for investigating chronic plastic changes, due to the short lifespan of rodents leading to a conflation of lesion- and neurodevelopmental- or aging-related plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the limitations of rodent models.

claim: Pre-lesion scans are rare in human studies and are mostly available in patients with pre-existing brain abnormalities.
source: In human studies, pre-lesion scans are rare and are mostly available in patients with pre-existing brain abnormalities, such as patients with epilepsy.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the availability of data in human studies.

claim: Mapping a lesion onto an atlas of connections could predict the remote areas affected and perhaps the behavioral consequences of a lesion.
source: It has recently been proposed that mapping a lesion onto an atlas of connections could predict the remote areas affected and perhaps the behavioral consequences of a lesion (Kuceyeski et al., 2014; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kuceyeski et al. (2014) and Thiebaut de Schotten et al. (2015).

claim: Hub regions are seemingly more likely to be affected in a variety of brain disorders.
source: Other studies have suggested that the role of brain regions within the whole brain architecture may be informative for the vulnerability to injury, with hub regions seemingly more likely to be affected in a variety of brain disorders (Crossley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Crossley et al. (2014).

claim: Hub regions may distribute resources following a brain injury in order to aid recovery in areas that are primarily affected by the injury.
source: This suggests the hypothesis that hub regions may distribute resources following a brain injury in order to aid recovery in areas that are primarily affected by the injury (Achard et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to Achard et al. (2012).

claim: There has been a resurgence in interest in large-scale gradients in cortical organization.
source: Recently, there has been a resurgence in interest in large-scale gradients in cortical organization (Beul et al., 2017; Burt et al., 2018; Goulas et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016; Markov et al., 2014; Sanides, 1962), and how this may enable cortical areas to specialize for distinct cognitive functions (Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Cortical gradients may enable cortical areas to specialize for distinct cognitive functions.
source: Recently, there has been a resurgence in interest in large-scale gradients in cortical organization (Beul et al., 2017; Burt et al., 2018; Goulas et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016; Markov et al., 2014; Sanides, 1962), and how this may enable cortical areas to specialize for distinct cognitive functions (Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chaudhuri et al. (2015).

claim: Neuron densities vary smoothly across the cortical surface.
source: Neuron densities vary smoothly across the cortical surface, with prefrontal cortex having less than half the neuron density of V1 (Collins et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Collins et al. (2010).

claim: Prefrontal cortex has less than half the neuron density of V1.
source: Neuron densities vary smoothly across the cortical surface, with prefrontal cortex having less than half the neuron density of V1 (Collins et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Collins et al. (2010).

claim: Astrocytes and microglia can have both beneficial and detrimental effects on post-injury plasticity.
source: Non-neuronal cells such as astrocytes and microglia can have both beneficial and detrimental effects on post-injury plasticity (Anderson et al., 2003; Loane and Kumar, 2016), and the exact distribution of these cells throughout the brain may also constrain or modulate the response of a region to injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al. (2003) and Loane and Kumar (2016).

claim: The exact distribution of astrocytes and microglia throughout the brain may constrain or modulate the response of a region to injury.
source: Non-neuronal cells such as astrocytes and microglia can have both beneficial and detrimental effects on post-injury plasticity (Anderson et al., 2003; Loane and Kumar, 2016), and the exact distribution of these cells throughout the brain may also constrain or modulate the response of a region to injury.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known effects of these cells and their distribution.

claim: This is the first study to demonstrate quantitatively a relationship between pre-lesion functional connectivity and the dynamic course of plasticity following a lesion.
source: This is the first study to demonstrate quantitatively a relationship between pre-lesion functional connectivity and the dynamic course of plasticity following a lesion and shows that information across a range of spatial scales can aid in prediction of the plastic recovery process following a lesion.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Information across a range of spatial scales can aid in prediction of the plastic recovery process following a lesion.
source: This is the first study to demonstrate quantitatively a relationship between pre-lesion functional connectivity and the dynamic course of plasticity following a lesion and shows that information across a range of spatial scales can aid in prediction of the plastic recovery process following a lesion.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings of the current study showing predictive value of multiple factors.

claim: The monkeys had a retrograde memory impairment but no anterograde memory impairment on the episodic memory task.
source: The monkeys had a retrograde memory impairment but no anterograde memory impairment on the episodic memory task.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral testing results described elsewhere (Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018).

claim: Isoflurane levels were kept to a minimum to ensure the preservation of resting-state networks.
source: For the resting-state fMRI scans, isoflurane levels were kept to a minimum to ensure the preservation of resting-state networks: mean isoflurane 1.2%, range 1.0–1.6% (Hutchison et al., 2014; Vincent et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hutchison et al. (2014) and Vincent et al. (2007).

claim: Resting-state fMRI was carried out at least 2 hr after ketamine administration to reduce detrimental effects of ketamine on resting-state networks.
source: Resting-state fMRI was carried out at least 2 hr after ketamine administration, to reduce detrimental effects of ketamine on resting-state networks (Bonhomme et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bonhomme et al. (2016).

claim: End-tidal CO2 was maintained in a normocapnic range to avoid effects of hypercapnia on the BOLD signal.
source: End-tidal CO2 was maintained in a normocapnic range wherever possible, to avoid effects of hypercapnia on the BOLD signal: mean CO2 39 mmHg, range 33–45 mmHg (Bandettini and Wong, 1997; Kastrup et al., 1999; Rostrup et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bandettini and Wong (1997), Kastrup et al. (1999), and Rostrup et al. (2000).

claim: The first principal component of node strength and network participation coefficient explained 73.19% of the variance.
source: As both network participation coefficient and node strength are proposed measures of hubness, and are positively correlated, we performed a principal components analysis on the strength and participation coefficient data, and took the first principal component, which explained 73.19% of the variance in strength and participation coefficient to be our estimate of hubness (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on principal components analysis of the data.

claim: The relationship between the acute and chronic stage changes to the network participation coefficient did not differ from chance.
source: The relationship between the acute and chronic stage changes to the network participation coefficient did not differ from chance (p = 0.66, corrected for the shared timepoint, see Materials and methods), suggesting that distinct degenerative and plastic processes affected network participation at the two stages.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis with p = 0.66.

claim: Distinct degenerative and plastic processes affected network participation at the acute and chronic stages.
source: The relationship between the acute and chronic stage changes to the network participation coefficient did not differ from chance (p = 0.66, corrected for the shared timepoint, see Materials and methods), suggesting that distinct degenerative and plastic processes affected network participation at the two stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of correlation between acute and chronic changes.

claim: Acute and chronic stage changes to within-module connectivity were more strongly positively associated than expected by chance.
source: Acute (Figure 4A) and chronic stage (Figure 4D) changes to within-module connectivity were more strongly positively associated than expected by chance (p < 0.001, corrected for the shared timepoint, see Materials and methods), suggesting that there may have been a continuation of degenerative or plastic processes from the acute to chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis with p < 0.001.

claim: There may have been a continuation of degenerative or plastic processes from the acute to chronic stage for within-module connectivity.
source: Acute (Figure 4A) and chronic stage (Figure 4D) changes to within-module connectivity were more strongly positively associated than expected by chance (p < 0.001, corrected for the shared timepoint, see Materials and methods), suggesting that there may have been a continuation of degenerative or plastic processes from the acute to chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the positive correlation between acute and chronic changes.

claim: Acute and chronic stage changes to cortical grey matter volume were more strongly positively associated than expected by chance.
source: Acute and chronic stage changes to cortical grey matter volume were more strongly positively associated than expected by chance (p = 0.01, corrected for the shared timepoint, see Materials and methods), suggesting that there may have been a continuation of degenerative grey matter loss from the acute to chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis with p = 0.01.

claim: There may have been a continuation of degenerative grey matter loss from the acute to chronic stage.
source: Acute and chronic stage changes to cortical grey matter volume were more strongly positively associated than expected by chance (p = 0.01, corrected for the shared timepoint, see Materials and methods), suggesting that there may have been a continuation of degenerative grey matter loss from the acute to chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the positive correlation between acute and chronic changes.

claim: Areas that were highly connected with the hippocampus before the lesion showed a drop in network participation during the acute stage.
source: Areas that were highly connected with the hippocampus before the lesion showed a drop in network participation during the acute stage, and a loss of grey matter volume over the chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analysis showing pre-lesion hippocampal connectivity as a significant predictor.

claim: Areas that were highly connected with the hippocampus before the lesion showed a loss of grey matter volume over the chronic stage.
source: Areas that were highly connected with the hippocampus before the lesion showed a drop in network participation during the acute stage, and a loss of grey matter volume over the chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analysis showing pre-lesion hippocampal connectivity as a significant predictor.

claim: Areas that were highly connected with the hippocampus before the lesion increased their functional connectivity with other areas in the same module over the chronic stage.
source: However, they also increased their functional connectivity with other areas in the same module over the chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analysis showing pre-lesion hippocampal connectivity as a significant predictor of chronic increases in within-module connectivity.

claim: MRI is sensitive to distinct microscale plasticity processes that occur during the acute and chronic stages post-lesion.
source: This may indicate that MRI is sensitive to distinct microscale plasticity processes that occur during the acute and chronic stages post-lesion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the different patterns of changes observed at acute and chronic stages.

claim: Network hubs showed a distinctive pattern of post-lesion alterations which suggested they are more vulnerable to the effects of the lesion.
source: Network hubs showed a distinctive pattern of post-lesion alterations, which suggested they are more vulnerable to the effects of the lesion.
evidence: The claim is based on the finding that hubness predicted drops in functional connectivity at both stages.

claim: The more a region acted as a hub in the pre-lesion network, the greater the reduction in functional connectivity at both the acute and chronic stages.
source: The more a region acted as a hub in the pre-lesion network, the greater the reduction in functional connectivity at both the acute and chronic stages.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analyses showing hubness as a significant predictor of connectivity reductions.

claim: Changes in activation in distant brain regions are widely agreed to be among the first adaptations following brain injury.
source: Changes in activation in distant brain regions are widely agreed to be among the first adaptations following brain injury before a return to more normal-appearing activation patterns in the spared tissue close to the affected site (Cramer, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cramer (2008).

claim: Connectomic information derived from databases of healthy humans has been used to identify remote areas likely to be affected by a lesion.
source: Recently in humans, connectomic information derived from databases of healthy humans has been used to identify remote areas likely to be affected by a lesion (Kuceyeski et al., 2014; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2015), but the relationship between the brain's connectivity profile and the dynamics of plasticity had not previously been investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kuceyeski et al. (2014) and Thiebaut de Schotten et al. (2015).

claim: The relationship between the brain's connectivity profile and the dynamics of plasticity had not previously been investigated.
source: Recently in humans, connectomic information derived from databases of healthy humans has been used to identify remote areas likely to be affected by a lesion (Kuceyeski et al., 2014; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2015), but the relationship between the brain's connectivity profile and the dynamics of plasticity had not previously been investigated.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the current study relative to prior work.

claim: Functional connectivity can be highly predictive of dynamic plastic changes in both the acute and chronic stages.
source: Here, we show that functional connectivity can be highly predictive of dynamic plastic changes in both the acute and chronic stages.
evidence: The claim is based on the regression analyses showing pre-lesion connectivity as a significant predictor.

claim: The functional connectivity loss and recovery may correspond to the timeline of loss and recovery of behavioral function following a lesion.
source: An intriguing possibility that should be investigated in larger future studies is that the functional connectivity loss and recovery may correspond to the timeline of loss and recovery of behavioral function following a lesion.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: Grayson and colleagues examined network changes in functional connectivity during reversible chemogenetic suppression of amygdala activity.
source: In a recent study, Grayson and colleagues examined network changes in functional connectivity during reversible chemogenetic suppression of amygdala activity (Grayson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Grayson et al. (2016).

claim: In the minutes and hours following amygdala suppression, network changes were detected with strong reduction in functional connectivity of the amygdala and its local modules.
source: In the minutes and hours following amygdala suppression, they were already able to detect some network changes, with strong reduction in functional connectivity of the amygdala and its local modules.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from Grayson et al. (2016).

claim: The global network structure is better preserved following chemogenetic disruption of the amygdala than following permanent lesions of the hippocampus.
source: On visual comparison of the force-directed graph plots of the current study (Figure 6) and the study of Grayson et al (their Figure 7), it appears that the global network structure is better preserved following chemogenetic disruption of the amygdala, than following permanent lesions of the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is based on visual comparison of results from the current study and Grayson et al. (2016).

claim: Permanent lesions are more likely to induce large-scale plasticity on the timescales of the present study than chemogenetic disruptions.
source: This is not particularly surprising as permanent lesions are more likely to induce large-scale plasticity, on the timescales of the present study.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the different effects of permanent vs. temporary disruptions.

claim: Focal hippocampal damage has widespread consequences beyond the immediate functional damage.
source: While lesions of the hippocampus have been implicated in human amnesia for decades (Corkin et al., 1997; Scoville and Milner, 1957), it is also clear that even focal hippocampal damage has widespread consequences beyond the immediate functional damage, and that memory is a distributed process that contains both segregation and overlap of function (Gaffan, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gaffan (2002).

claim: Memory is a distributed process that contains both segregation and overlap of function.
source: While lesions of the hippocampus have been implicated in human amnesia for decades (Corkin et al., 1997; Scoville and Milner, 1957), it is also clear that even focal hippocampal damage has widespread consequences beyond the immediate functional damage, and that memory is a distributed process that contains both segregation and overlap of function (Gaffan, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gaffan (2002).

claim: The concept of connectional diaschisis has been identified in human patients with focal hippocampal damage.
source: This concept of connectional diaschisis (Carrera and Tononi, 2014) has also been identified in human patients with focal hippocampal damage, where the functional alterations to a network extended far beyond the structural damage (Henson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carrera and Tononi (2014) and Henson et al. (2016).

claim: In human patients with focal hippocampal damage, functional alterations to a network extended far beyond the structural damage.
source: This concept of connectional diaschisis (Carrera and Tononi, 2014) has also been identified in human patients with focal hippocampal damage, where the functional alterations to a network extended far beyond the structural damage (Henson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Henson et al. (2016).

claim: The initial phase of an ischemic event leads to excitotoxic death via activation of glutamate receptors.
source: The initial phase of an ischemic event, for example, leads to excitotoxic death via activation of glutamate receptors, as in our deliberate NMDA lesion, but this is only one of a cascade of processes (Cramer, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cramer (2008).

claim: The mechanisms involved in traumatic brain injury start with cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure.
source: The mechanisms involved in traumatic brain injury are less similar to our excitotoxic lesions, starting with cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure, followed by a number of other factors of which glutamate excitotoxicity is just one (Kinoshita, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kinoshita (2016).

claim: NMDA-induced lesions spare fibers of passage within or adjacent to the area.
source: The strength of a specific NMDA-induced lesion, which spares fibers of passage within or adjacent to the area (Coffey et al., 1988; Köhler and Schwarcz, 1983) is that we can study the effect of damage to a specific area on the rest of the brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coffey et al. (1988) and Köhler and Schwarcz (1983).

claim: The medial septum, amygdala and posterior parahippocampal cortex and the white matter tracts connecting them to the hippocampus are affected in human subjects with developmental amnesia.
source: We observed decreases in the volume of the medial septum, amygdala and posterior parahippocampal cortex. These regions and the white matter tracts connecting them to the hippocampus are also affected in human subjects with developmental amnesia (Dzieciol et al., 2017; Olsen et al., 2013) and in people born very preterm (Ball et al., 2012; Caldinelli et al., 2017; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2017; Salvan et al., 2014; Tseng et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dzieciol et al. (2017) and Olsen et al. (2013).

claim: The medial septum, amygdala and posterior parahippocampal cortex and the white matter tracts connecting them to the hippocampus are affected in people born very preterm.
source: We observed decreases in the volume of the medial septum, amygdala and posterior parahippocampal cortex. These regions and the white matter tracts connecting them to the hippocampus are also affected in human subjects with developmental amnesia (Dzieciol et al., 2017; Olsen et al., 2013) and in people born very preterm (Ball et al., 2012; Caldinelli et al., 2017; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2017; Salvan et al., 2014; Tseng et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ball et al. (2012), Caldinelli et al. (2017), Froudist-Walsh et al. (2017), Salvan et al. (2014), and Tseng et al. (2017).

claim: Severe structural abnormalities associated with developmental amnesia lead to seemingly permanent impairments to episodic memory.
source: Although the severe structural abnormalities associated with developmental amnesia lead to seemingly permanent impairments to episodic memory (Vargha-Khadem et al., 2001), milder damage to this circuit may enable plastic changes in cortical functional connectivity to partially compensate for damage to the core episodic memory circuit (Isaacs et al., 2003; Nosarti and Froudist-Walsh, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vargha-Khadem et al. (2001).

claim: Milder damage to the episodic memory circuit may enable plastic changes in cortical functional connectivity to partially compensate for damage to the core episodic memory circuit.
source: Although the severe structural abnormalities associated with developmental amnesia lead to seemingly permanent impairments to episodic memory (Vargha-Khadem et al., 2001), milder damage to this circuit may enable plastic changes in cortical functional connectivity to partially compensate for damage to the core episodic memory circuit (Isaacs et al., 2003; Nosarti and Froudist-Walsh, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Isaacs et al. (2003) and Nosarti and Froudist-Walsh (2016).

claim: Incomplete damage to subcortical structures such as the mammillary bodies, fornix and connected thalamic subregions in combination with plastic changes to spared areas may be crucial for the preservation or recovery of anterograde memory abilities.
source: In the present study, the incomplete damage to subcortical structures such as the mammillary bodies, fornix and connected thalamic subregions in combination with plastic changes to spared areas may be crucial for the preservation or recovery or anterograde memory abilities (Baxter, 2013; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baxter (2013), Froudist-Walsh et al. (2018), and Mitchell et al. (2008).

claim: The study design cannot distinguish between compensatory and maladaptive plasticity.
source: Nonetheless, we acknowledge a limitation of the study is that our design cannot distinguish between compensatory and maladaptive plasticity.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study design.

claim: Dendritic tree size and spine count tend to show opposite gradients to neuron density.
source: Dendritic tree size and spine count tend to show opposite gradients to neuron density, with lowest values in early visual cortex and peaking in higher association areas (Elston et al., 2010; Scholtens et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elston et al. (2010) and Scholtens et al. (2014).

claim: The loss of connectivity in areas with higher neuron density may be reflective of a lack of dendritic spines that can be crucial for synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus the loss of connectivity in areas with higher neuron density may be reflective of other factors, such as a lack of dendritic spines that can be crucial for synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the relationship between neuron density and dendritic spine density.

claim: Local and distant remodeling of spines and dendritic trees has been observed following stroke.
source: Indeed, local and distant remodeling of spines and dendritic trees has been observed following stroke (Brown et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2010; Nudo, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown et al. (2007), Brown et al. (2010), and Nudo (2013).

claim: Synaptic plasticity is traditionally thought of as being neuronally initiated.
source: Although synaptic plasticity is traditionally thought of as being neuronally initiated, it is now clear that astrocytes and microglia can modify synaptic connectivity in a variety of ways (Ben Achour and Pascual, 2010; Allen and Barres, 2005; Araque et al., 1999; Ullian et al., 2004) and can even alter synaptic strength in the absence of neuronal activity (Clark et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a statement about traditional views in the field.

claim: Astrocytes and microglia can modify synaptic connectivity in a variety of ways.
source: Although synaptic plasticity is traditionally thought of as being neuronally initiated, it is now clear that astrocytes and microglia can modify synaptic connectivity in a variety of ways (Ben Achour and Pascual, 2010; Allen and Barres, 2005; Araque et al., 1999; Ullian et al., 2004) and can even alter synaptic strength in the absence of neuronal activity (Clark et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ben Achour and Pascual (2010), Allen and Barres (2005), Araque et al. (1999), and Ullian et al. (2004).

claim: Astrocytes and microglia can alter synaptic strength in the absence of neuronal activity.
source: Although synaptic plasticity is traditionally thought of as being neuronally initiated, it is now clear that astrocytes and microglia can modify synaptic connectivity in a variety of ways (Ben Achour and Pascual, 2010; Allen and Barres, 2005; Araque et al., 1999; Ullian et al., 2004) and can even alter synaptic strength in the absence of neuronal activity (Clark et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Clark et al. (2015).

claim: Astrocytes and microglia have emerged as promising candidates for treatment following acquired brain injury in humans.
source: Astrocytes and microglia can have both beneficial and detrimental effects on post-injury plasticity (Anderson et al., 2003; Loane and Kumar, 2016) and have emerged as promising candidates for treatment following acquired brain injury in humans (Barreto et al., 2011; Loane and Kumar, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barreto et al. (2011) and Loane and Kumar (2016).

claim: Non-neuronal cell density positively correlates with the increase in the network participation coefficient during the chronic stage, providing a novel link between the local role of glia at the synapse and plasticity of large-scale functional connectivity patterns.
source: Our finding that non-neuronal cell density positively correlates with the increase in the network participation coefficient during the chronic stage provides a novel link between the local role of glia at the synapse, and plasticity of large-scale functional connectivity patterns.
evidence: The claim is based on the regression analysis showing non-neuronal cell density as a significant predictor.

claim: Hub regions are more likely to lose functional connectivity following a lesion, even if the primary site of injury is not itself a hub.
source: Here we show that hub regions are in fact more likely to suffer a loss of functional connectivity, even if the primary site of injury – the hippocampus – is not itself a hub.
evidence: The claim is based on the regression analyses showing hubness as a significant predictor of connectivity loss.

claim: Hubs are more likely to be connected to the site of primary insult and more likely to suffer from diaschisis as a result.
source: An extension of that hypothesis is that hubs are more likely to be connected to the site of primary insult (in this case the hippocampus), and more likely to suffer from diaschisis as a result.
evidence: The claim is presented as an extension of a hypothesis from Crossley et al. (2014).

claim: Hubness was an independent predictor of structural and functional losses following a lesion, even after accounting for the effects of functional connectivity to the lesioned area.
source: We showed that 'hubness' was an independent predictor of structural and functional losses following a lesion, even after accounting for the effects of functional connectivity to the lesioned area.
evidence: The claim is based on the regression analyses where both hubness and hippocampal connectivity were included as predictors.

claim: The degradation of the hubs was associated with a destruction of the overall network structure in the chronic stage.
source: The degradation of the hubs was also associated with a destruction of the overall network structure in the chronic stage.
evidence: The claim is based on the observed increase in modularity and decrease in number of modules.

claim: At 12 months following the lesion, the whole brain network had separated into a smaller number of weakly interconnected modules.
source: At 12 months following the lesion, the whole brain network had separated into a smaller number of weakly interconnected modules.
evidence: The claim is based on module detection analysis showing fewer modules and increased modularity.

claim: Focal lesions can have effects on global brain function.
source: This demonstrates effects that focal lesions can have on global brain function.
evidence: The claim is based on the observed changes in network structure following hippocampal lesions.

claim: Hubs may have a relatively high neuron to non-neuronal cell ratio, perhaps indicating a lack of glial and other support cells per neuron.
source: Speculatively, in an exploratory analysis, we found a relatively high neuron: non-neuronal cell ratio in hubs, perhaps indicating a lack of glial other support cells per neuron.
evidence: The claim is based on exploratory regression analysis and is presented as speculative.

claim: Hubs may be less able to adapt to injury than non-hub areas due to a lack of glial and other support cells per neuron.
source: Speculatively, in an exploratory analysis, we found a relatively high neuron: non-neuronal cell ratio in hubs, perhaps indicating a lack of glial other support cells per neuron. This may mean that hubs are less able to adapt to injury than non-hub areas.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the exploratory analysis and is presented as speculative.

claim: Consistent relationships between cell densities and hub properties have yet to emerge across different studies.
source: Several studies have recently examined the relationships between cell densities and hub properties yet consistent relationships have yet to emerge, perhaps due to the use of different experimental techniques and definitions of hubs across different species (Beul et al., 2015; Beul et al., 2017; van den Heuvel et al., 2015; Rubinov et al., 2015; Scholtens et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing inconsistent results.

claim: The specific cellular composition of the hippocampus may have played a role in the patterns of plasticity observed.
source: Given our finding that plasticity following a lesion is highly dependent on the cellular composition of different brain regions, it may be the case that the specific cellular composition of the hippocampus may also have played a role in the patterns of plasticity we see here.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative possibility based on the study findings.

claim: The unique connectivity of the hippocampus relative to other brain regions may be an important factor in the patterns of plasticity observed.
source: The unique connectivity of the hippocampus relative to other brain regions may also be an important factor.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative possibility.

claim: Different patterns of plasticity may be observed following lesions to other brain regions.
source: This suggests that we may see very different patterns of plasticity following lesions to other brain regions.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative inference from the study findings.

claim: Functional and structural changes can greatly differ between acute and chronic stages following a lesion.
source: Firstly, we show that functional and structural changes can greatly differ between acute and chronic stages.
evidence: The claim is based on the different patterns of changes observed at the two time points.

claim: Post-lesion plasticity patterns depend on pre-lesion functional connectivity.
source: Secondly, while it has been known for some time that areas connected to a lesioned brain region are more likely to be affected by the lesion than non-connected areas, to our knowledge this is the first study to show quantitatively that post-lesion plasticity patterns depend on pre-lesion functional connectivity.
evidence: The claim is based on the regression analyses showing pre-lesion connectivity as a significant predictor.

claim: Microstructural gradients and macrostructural network measures can provide additional predictive value and insights into the plasticity process.
source: Lastly, we link across spatial scales, and show how microstructural gradients and macrostructural network measures can provide additional predictive value and insights into the plasticity process.
evidence: The claim is based on the regression analyses showing cell densities and hubness as significant predictors.
